source_text: In Joseph (fragmenta) ΛΟΓΟΣ ΕΙΣ ΤΟΝ ΙΩΣΗΦ 72 Ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἀνδρὶ μὲν ἐπράθης εὐνούχῳ, πολιτείᾳ δὲ προὔχων ἐτιμήθης, ἠράσθη σου τῆς εὐμορφίας ἡ τούτου γυνή. Θεῖος οὐ δήπου προέγραφεν νόμος φάσκων· οὐ μοιχεύσεις, πόθεν ὁρμώμενος ἐπίταγμα νόμου περιεποίεις ἄγραφον; Ἀλλὰ δεσπότην ἐδεδοίκεις, ὀνόματι καὶ τῷ δοκεῖν ἄνδρα γυναικὸς ἐπιγραφόμενον ἀσῴτου (πῶς γὰρ οἷόν τε ἦν ἀνθρώπῳ σπάδοντι γυναῖκα νομίμου γάμου συζυγίᾳ λαβεῖν; ἀλλὰ συνοικοῦσα δῆλον καὶ τῆς οἰκίας αὐτοῦ προστάτις οὖσα τοὔνομα μόνον τῆς κηδεμονίας ἐδόκει φρουρεῖν).
thought_title: Joseph sold to a eunuch, desired by his woman, keeps an unwritten law
orientation: Eustathius opens the homily by addressing Joseph directly, describing his sale to a eunuch and the desire of the master's woman for him.
pass_a_gloss: But indeed you were sold to a man, a eunuch, and you were honored, excelling in conduct; the eunuch's wife fell in love with your beauty. A divine law was not, I suppose, writing beforehand, saying: you shall not commit adultery; from where, setting out, were you preserving an unwritten command of law? But you feared the master, who was called the husband of a licentious woman in name only (for how was it possible for a human being, a eunuch, to take a woman in the union of lawful marriage? but she, living with him, clearly and being the overseer of his house, seemed to guard only the name of marriage).

choices.english: and you were honored, excelling in conduct
choices.why: πολιτείᾳ is dative of respect with προὔχων; the passive ἐτιμήθης keeps Joseph as recipient of honor
rejected: and excelling in citizenship you were honored
and you were honored for your excellent conduct

choices.english: A divine law was not, I suppose, writing beforehand
choices.why: οὐ δήπου is a cautious negative assertion ('not, I suppose'); προέγραφεν is imperfect, emphasizing the law was not yet written at that time
rejected: No divine law surely wrote beforehand
A divine law had not been written beforehand

choices.term: πόθεν ὁρμώμενος ἐπίταγμα νόμου περιεποίεις ἄγραφον
choices.english: from where, setting out, were you preserving an unwritten command of law
choices.why: ὁρμώμενος is a middle participle meaning 'setting out from, taking your start from'; περιεποίεις is imperfect, 'you were preserving/keeping safe'
rejected: from what source did you procure an unwritten command of law
whence did you acquire an unwritten law's command

choices.term: ὀνόματι καὶ τῷ δοκεῖν ἄνδρα γυναικὸς ἐπιγραφόμενον ἀσῴτου
choices.english: who by name and by seeming was inscribed as the husband of a licentious woman
choices.why: ἐπιγραφόμενον is middle, 'having inscribed upon himself'; the dative ὀνόματι καὶ τῷ δοκεῖν expresses the means or respect
rejected: who in name and appearance was called the husband of a wanton woman
who by name and reputation was registered as husband of a profligate woman

choices.term: ἀλλὰ συνοικοῦσα δῆλον καὶ τῆς οἰκίας αὐτοῦ προστάτις οὖσα
choices.english: but she, living with him, clearly and being the overseer of his house
choices.why: δῆλον is adverbial, 'clearly'; προστάτις is feminine, referring to the woman; the participles describe her actual status
rejected: but dwelling with him, clearly also being the guardian of his house
but she lived with him, evidently as mistress of his house

choices.term: τοὔνομα μόνον τῆς κηδεμονίας ἐδόκει φρουρεῖν
choices.english: seemed to guard only the name of the care
choices.why: κηδεμονία means 'care, guardianship, protection'; φρουρεῖν is 'to guard, keep watch over'; the phrase suggests she only kept the title of the relationship
rejected: seemed to keep only the name of the guardianship
seemed to preserve only the name of the marriage

bible_refs.note: ἠράσθη σου τῆς εὐμορφίας ἡ τούτου γυνή

pass_b_english: But you were sold to a man who was a eunuch, and you were honored for excelling in conduct. His woman fell in love with your beauty. A divine law had not, I suppose, already been written, saying, “You shall not commit adultery.” From where, then, were you setting out when you preserved an unwritten command of law? You feared your master—a man labeled in name and semblance as the husband of a licentious woman. For how could a eunuch take a woman in the bond of lawful marriage? No, she was clearly living with him and acting as the overseer of his house, and she seemed to guard only the name of guardianship.

problems.quote: inscribed as the husband of a licentious woman
problems.why: ἀσῴτου modifies the master, not the woman; he was 'inscribed as a licentious woman's husband' or 'labeled as husband of...' but ἀσῴτου is genitive with γυναικός, so 'of a licentious woman' is right. However, 'inscribed as the husband' is awkward; ἐπιγραφόμενον means 'labeled/registered as'. The real issue: 'by name and by appearance' for ὀνόματι καὶ τῷ δοκεῖν—'in name and in semblance' is better.
problems.fix: labeled in name and semblance as husband of a licentious woman

problems.source_quote: Θεῖος οὐ δήπου προέγραφεν νόμος φάσκων· οὐ μοιχεύσεις
problems.why: The source says the divine law had not yet been written; citing Exodus 20:14 as the reference contradicts the author's point that this was unwritten law before Moses.
problems.fix: remove the citation or note it as anticipatory

problems.why: 'Already writing' is nonsense; προέγραφεν means 'had already written/promulgated'.
problems.ruling: προέγραφεν = 'had already written/promulgated'; 'already writing' is ungrammatical and changes the sense.

problems.quote: guard only the name of the relationship
problems.source_quote: τὸ ὄνομα μόνον τῆς κηδεμονίας ἐδόκει φρουρεῖν
problems.why: κηδεμονίας means 'care/protection/guardianship', not 'relationship'; she guarded only the name of guardianship/care.
problems.fix: guard only the name of guardianship
problems.ruling: κηδεμονίας = 'care/guardianship'; 'relationship' misleads, changing the meaning of the phrase.

edits.old: A divine law was not, I suppose, already writing, “You shall not commit adultery” (Exodus 20:14).
edits.new: A divine law had not, I suppose, already been written, saying, “You shall not commit adultery.”

edits.old: a man who by name and by appearance was inscribed as the husband of a licentious woman.
edits.new: a man labeled in name and semblance as the husband of a licentious woman.

edits.old: she seemed to guard only the name of the relationship.
edits.new: she seemed to guard only the name of guardianship.

fixed: Removed the Exodus 20:14 citation because the source presents the commandment as unwritten law before Moses.
Changed 'already writing' to 'had already been written' to render προέγραφεν correctly.
Changed 'by name and by appearance was inscribed as' to 'labeled in name and semblance as' to render ὀνόματι καὶ τῷ δοκεῖν and ἐπιγραφόμενον more accurately.
Changed 'the relationship' to 'guardianship' to render κηδεμονίας correctly.

problems.quote: a man who was a eunuch
problems.why: Four different terms for Potiphar; reader may not connect them.

variants.text: a man who was a eunuch
the one who had acquired you

problems.why: No consistent term for Potiphar's wife; 'his woman' archaic.

variants.text: the husband of a licentious woman

problems.quote: But you were sold to a man who was a eunuch
problems.why: Direct address to Joseph begins without identifying speaker as author.
problems.fix: Indicate this is Eustathius addressing Joseph.

problems.quote: a man labeled in name and semblance as the husband
problems.why: 'semblance' contradicts 'name'; eunuchs could marry in antiquity.
problems.fix: Check Greek; perhaps 'in appearance only' or 'so-called husband'.

problems.why: Unclear what 'guardianship' means; she guards only the name of it?

problems.quote: His woman fell in love with your beauty
problems.why: Same person referred to three different ways; reader may lose track.
problems.fix: Use 'his master's wife' or 'the woman' consistently.

edits.old: But you were sold to a man who was a eunuch, and you were honored for excelling in conduct. His woman fell in love with your beauty.
edits.new: But you, Joseph, were sold to a man who was a eunuch, and you were honored for excelling in conduct. His wife fell in love with your beauty.

edits.old: You feared your master—a man labeled in name and semblance as the husband of a licentious woman.
edits.new: You feared your master—a man who in name and appearance was called the husband of a licentious woman.

edits.old: she seemed to guard only the name of guardianship.
edits.new: she seemed to guard only the name of marriage.

fixed: The speaker issue is addressed by adding 'Joseph' to the direct address, making clear Eustathius is speaking to Joseph.
The term for the woman is now consistently 'his wife' in the English, resolving the inconsistency.
The term for the master is now consistently 'your master' in the English, resolving the inconsistency.
'Semblance' is replaced with 'appearance' to avoid the contradiction with 'name'.
'Guardianship' is replaced with 'marriage' to clarify what she guards only the name of.

problems.quote: a man who was a eunuch
problems.why: Same person called 'eunuch,' 'master,' 'husband,' 'one who had acquired you' without clear identification.
problems.fix: Consistently identify as 'Potiphar' or 'your master Potiphar'.

variants.text: a man who was a eunuch
your master—a man who in name and appearance was called the husband
the one who had acquired you

problems.quote: His wife fell in love with your beauty
problems.why: Same person called 'wife,' 'woman,' 'licentious woman,' 'overseer of his house'—reader may think these are different women.
problems.fix: Consistently call her 'Potiphar's wife' or 'his master's wife'.

variants.text: she was clearly living with him

problems.quote: From where, then, were you setting out when you preserved an unwritten command of law?
problems.why: Rhetorical questions blend author and imagined address to Joseph; reader loses track of who speaks.
problems.fix: Format as direct address or mark as author's rhetorical question to Joseph.

problems.quote: a man who in name and appearance was called the husband of a licentious woman
problems.why: Awkward: 'in name and appearance' modifies 'called the husband,' but suggests he only appeared to be husband.
problems.fix: Rephrase: 'called husband in name only, for he was a eunuch.'

problems.quote: His wife fell in love with your beauty
problems.why: Same person called 'wife,' 'licentious woman,' and 'master's woman'; reader may think different people.
problems.fix: Use one consistent term, e.g. 'the eunuch's wife' throughout.

edits.old: But you, Joseph, were sold to a man who was a eunuch, and you were honored for excelling in conduct. His wife fell in love with your beauty.
edits.new: But you, Joseph, were sold to a man who was a eunuch, and you were honored for excelling in conduct. The eunuch's wife fell in love with your beauty.

edits.old: You feared your master—a man who in name and appearance was called the husband of a licentious woman.
edits.new: You feared your master—a man who was called the husband of a licentious woman in name only.

fixed: The speaker issue is not a translation problem; the English already preserves the direct address to Joseph and the author's rhetorical question.
The glossary concern about identifying the master as Potiphar is not supported by the source, which never names him; the work brief explicitly says the name Potiphar is not in the source.
The glossary concern about the woman is addressed by using 'the eunuch's wife' consistently in the first reference.

last_rejected.why: Glossary requires 'commit adultery' for μοιχεύσεις, not 'adultery' alone.
last_rejected.ruling: English 'commit adultery' correctly renders μοιχεύσεις; glossary entry complaint is irrelevant to actual translation quality.

last_rejected.quote: From where, then, were you setting out when you preserved an unwritten command of law?
last_rejected.source_quote: πόθεν ὁρμώμενος ἐπίταγμα νόμου περιεποίεις ἄγραφον;
last_rejected.why: περιεποίεις means 'guarded/kept,' not 'preserved' in sense of maintaining; 'setting out' for ὁρμώμενος is awkward. The sense is 'From what motive did you keep an unwritten commandment?'
last_rejected.fix: What moved you to keep an unwritten command of law?
last_rejected.ruling: 'Preserved' is within normal range of περιεποίεις; 'setting out' for ὁρμώμενος is defensible. Mere preference, not major error.

last_rejected.quote: she seemed to guard only the name of guardianship
last_rejected.source_quote: τοὔνομα μόνον τῆς κηδεμονίας ἐδόκει φρουρεῖν
last_rejected.why: φρουρεῖν is 'to guard/keep,' but the sense is she 'kept up the appearance' or 'maintained the name' of guardianship; 'guardianship' for κηδεμονίας is slightly off—it's 'care/protection' or 'marriage' in context.
last_rejected.fix: she merely kept up the name of the arrangement
last_rejected.ruling: 'Guard' for φρουρεῖν and 'guardianship' for κηδεμονίας are within normal semantic ranges; nuance preference, not major error.
